items.summary: Slip Op. 26-140, an Opinion and Order dated November 19, 2026, by Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves of the U.S. Court of International Trade in Oman Aluminium Rolling Company SPC v. United States, remands the U.S. Department of Commerce's final results of the 2022-2023 antidumping duty administrative review of certain aluminum foil from the Sultanate of Oman, published at 90 Fed. Reg. 44,162 on September 12, 2025. The opinion recounts the review's procedural history, including Commerce's questionnaires, a 90-day tolling of deadlines beginning December 9, 2024, the suspension of the briefing schedule on January 10, 2025, the acceptance of new factual information, and the Final Issues and Decision Memorandum issued September 8, 2025. It cites 19 U.S.C. § 1516a for jurisdiction and begins a discussion of facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e, and the source text is truncated before that discussion concludes.

Cordeus Rainey, No. 26-1621, that the court had issued an opinion and entered judgment. The letter states that petitions for rehearing and rehearing en banc must be received within 14 days of the entry of judgment, must be filed electronically in CM/ECF, and carry no mailing grace period except as provided by FRAP 25(a)(2)(iii). It adds that a petition not received within the FRAP 40 period may be denied as untimely.

items.summary: In this nonprecedential per curiam decision issued November 20, 2026, the Federal Circuit addressed a petition for review by Mohammad Khaghani of a Merit Systems Protection Board final order denying corrective action in an individual right of action appeal against the Department of the Navy. The Board had found two of eight alleged disclosures protected but determined that the agency showed by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same personnel actions absent those disclosures. The court affirmed, finding no error in the Board's legal standards or its credibility determinations.

items.summary: In this unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 20, 2026, the Fifth Circuit reviewed a summary judgment for the City of Lexington, Mississippi and its police officers in a suit by Peter Reeves arising from a traffic roadblock stop. The panel held that Heck v. Humphrey continues to bar the damages claim, and reversed the judgment as to injunctive relief in light of Olivier v. City of Brandon, 607 U.S. 552 (2026), remanding for further proceedings. Judge Oldham concurred in the judgment, addressing the damages claim under the favorable-termination requirement.

items.summary: In this nonprecedential opinion issued November 20, 2026, the Federal Circuit affirmed a Patent Trial and Appeal Board final written decision in an appeal by Ollnova Technologies Ltd. from inter partes reviews brought by Copeland Comfort Control LP and ecobee Technologies ULC. The Board held claims 1, 3-8, 14, 15, and 18 of U.S. Patent No. 7,746,887 unpatentable as obvious, and construed 'suspended' in claim 1 to encompass both suspension of an otherwise-occurring transmission and the absence of transmission when a change does not exceed a limit. items.summary: In this nonprecedential decision issued November 20, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed three final decisions of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board in inter partes reviews of U.S. Patent No. 10,447,450, owned by Neo Wireless LLC, in appeals by American Honda Motor Co., Inc. and Tesla, Inc. items.summary: The D.C. Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Mercuria Energy Group's petition to enforce a Swedish arbitration award against the Republic of Poland under the New York Convention and the Federal Arbitration Act. The court held that the Swedish appellate court's annulment of the award was not repugnant to fundamental notions of what is decent and just in the United States, and it rejected the appellant's reliance on the Second Circuit's decision in Pemex. In a concurring opinion, Senior Circuit Judge Randolph wrote that the court's Getma and TermoRio formulations deserve reconsideration, while acknowledging that precedent requires adherence to them.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit held that the Board of Immigration Appeals did not abuse its discretion in denying Juana Elizalde Castillo and her sons' motions to reopen and to reconsider their removal proceedings. The court found that Castillo did not identify an error of law or fact, and did not establish a prima facie case for asylum relief or a material change in country conditions. The court also ordered Castillo's counsel to show cause why sanctions should not be imposed, citing suspected use of generative artificial intelligence in the briefs.

items.summary: The D.C. Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the Navy in Nicholas Voegeli's suit challenging the denial of his nomination for the Navy and Marine Corps Medal. The court held that the Board for Correction of Naval Records' refusal to waive the Navy policy requiring two eyewitness statements was not arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. The court reasoned that Voegeli's own account, a summary of action, and an affidavit attesting to earlier eyewitness statements did not supply the required eyewitness evidence.

items.summary: In a nonprecedential order decided November 20, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the defendants in Sean Paul Reyes's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit arising from his 2021 arrest for disorderly conduct while recording inside Berwyn, Illinois city hall. The court held that undisputed evidence established probable cause for the arrest under 720 ILCS 5/26-1(a)(1) and that the edited video did not support Reyes's claim that his conduct was reasonable and nondisruptive. Because probable cause existed, the court found that his conspiracy and malicious prosecution claims also failed.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit vacated the district court's order dismissing Maurice Hardaway's pro se 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit as time-barred and remanded the case. The court held that if Hardaway tendered an amended complaint to prison staff on July 17, 2025, it would be timely under the prison mailbox rule, and directed the district court to determine whether it was timely filed. The order also notes that dismissals at screening on limitations grounds are generally brought under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(c) or 56(c) rather than 12(b)(6), unless the complaint's allegations preclude tolling.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit denied the petition for review filed by a Guatemalan mother and her minor daughter, who challenged a Board of Immigration Appeals decision denying asylum. The court held that the record did not compel a finding that the Guatemalan government was unable or unwilling to protect the mother from private actors, namely her husband and his family, and that the police had previously issued and delivered a restraining order. The court did not reach the Board's alternative grounds for denial and noted that an argument under a class action settlement was not exhausted before the Board.

items.summary: In a not-recommended-for-publication opinion filed November 20, 2026, in appeal No. 26-5972, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit dismissed appeals filed by Timothy Ehn, a defendant convicted of health-care fraud, and denied as moot his motion to stay the sale of real estate held by GT Enterprise, LLC. The court held that the appeal of the sale order was untimely under the 14-day deadline of Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)(1)(A)(i) and that Ehn lacked Article III standing to appeal the stay order because his interest in GT Enterprise became property of his Chapter 7 bankruptcy estate. The opinion was issued by Circuit Judges Gilman, Davis, and Mathis.

items.summary: In this unpublished Sixth Circuit per curiam opinion, the court vacated a judgment entered for correctional officer Evan Barton in an Eighth Amendment failure-to-protect case brought by state inmate Brandon Schiefel, and remanded. The court held that the district court abused its discretion by excluding testimony from two fellow inmates that Schiefel had told Barton about a prior fight with another inmate, because the testimony was offered to show Barton's knowledge rather than the truth of the matter asserted and was therefore not hearsay. The court remanded for the district court to determine in the first instance whether the exclusion affected Schiefel's substantial rights.
items.title: Brandon Schiefel v. Evan Barton, et al

items.summary: In a not-recommended-for-publication opinion filed November 20, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit considered Alfredo Cazales-Lopez's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision that denied his application for cancellation of removal. The court stated that it lacked jurisdiction over his challenges to the immigration judge's factual findings and rejected his remaining legal arguments on the merits. The court dismissed the petition in part and denied it in part.
items.title: Alfredo Cazales-Lopez v. Todd Blanche

items.summary: In this unpublished Sixth Circuit opinion, the court affirmed a 78-month sentence imposed on Avery Logan after he pleaded guilty to unlawful firearm possession under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). The district court applied an attempted-murder Guidelines cross-reference, which produced a recommended range of 100 to 125 months, and then imposed a below-range sentence after varying downward. The court rejected Logan's challenges to the cross-reference, holding that his argument that the district court made no express intent finding was not preserved, and it also rejected his facial and as-applied challenges to § 922(g)(1).
items.title: USA v. Avery Logan

items.summary: In this unpublished Sixth Circuit opinion, the court affirmed a sentence for firearm convictions in which the district court applied the attempted first-degree murder cross-reference, yielding a base offense level of 33. The case arose from a shooting in which Smith and companions followed a driver home after a verbal altercation at a traffic intersection and fired 19 rounds at him while he sat in his car. The court held that the undisputed facts showed premeditation, pointing to the timeline, including the decision to follow the victim home, and the absence of any sudden provocation immediately before the shooting.
items.title: USA v. Robert Smith, II

items.summary: In this unpublished Sixth Circuit opinion, the court affirmed the Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint filed by Rick Stover, a former Oakland County Jail inmate, against Oakland County, Sheriff Michael Bouchard, and unnamed John Doe deputies. The complaint alleged that jail personnel withheld medication Stover needed, which he claimed led to atrial fibrillation. The court held that the complaint did not plead a County policy or custom under Monell, did not allege Bouchard's own individual conduct or a failure-to-train claim, and did not plead facts showing deliberate indifference by the John Doe deputies.
items.title: Rick Stover v. Michael Bouchard, et al

items.summary: In this Sixth Circuit opinion, the court affirmed a judgment for the United States against Norman Rhodes for unpaid income taxes, penalties, and interest, which the district court set at $558,352.96 plus interest. The court concluded that the income deposited into the 'Signmaker' and 'Graphic Associates' accounts belonged to Rhodes and that the 'July Thirtyfirst' entity did not qualify as a trust under Michigan law. The judgment also directed the sale of Rhodes's Harsens Island home to satisfy the debt.
items.title: USA v. Norman Rhodes, et al

items.summary: In this unpublished Sixth Circuit opinion, the court affirmed a 188-month prison sentence imposed on Dontrell Wilson after he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a felon. Reviewing for plain error, the court considered Wilson's challenges to a supervised-release condition permitting a probation officer to search his electronic devices upon reasonable suspicion of a violation and to a $500 fine. The court held that the search condition was reasonably related to the offense and criminal history, that the district court reasonably found Wilson could pay the fine through prison work, and that no plain error occurred.

items.summary: S. 3885, the Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act, was introduced February 12, 2026, by Senator Welch and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. The reported version, by Senator Cruz with an amendment, is Report No. 119-166. The bill directs the FAA Administrator to publish a plan on type certification process improvements, to amend FAA Order 8110.112A to establish standard expected timelines, and to set criteria for issue papers and updated delegation guidance, with a rule of construction stating that those timelines create no new legal right and are not subject to judicial review.
